name: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Caused by vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, which preferentially damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord
Typically presents with symmetrical distal paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint-position sense, and a progressive spastic-ataxic gait
Combines upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, extensor plantars) with impaired proprioception and sometimes absent ankle reflexes, giving a mixed picture
Neuropsychiatric features such as cognitive slowing, irritability, or depression may accompany or precede the myelopathy
Serum B12 can be borderline or normal, so raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are more sensitive markers of tissue deficiency
Common causes include pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, strict vegan diet, gastric surgery, and prolonged nitrous oxide exposure
Early replacement of B12 can halt and partially reverse deficits; delayed treatment risks permanent disability
Macrocytic anaemia may be absent, so neurological disease can occur without haematological changes
reference.pathophysiology: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Deficiency impairs myelin synthesis and maintenance, leading to vacuolar demyelination and axonal degeneration that begins in the dorsal columns and later involves the lateral (corticospinal) columns, hence the term 'combined'. Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin and can precipitate the disorder in those with marginal stores. The pathology accounts for the combination of sensory ataxia from posterior column loss and spasticity from corticospinal tract involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating myelopathy
Compressive cervical myelopathy or spondylotic myelopathy
Tabes dorsalis and other causes of sensory ataxia
additionalInvestigations: Serum vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when B12 is borderline
Full blood count and blood film for macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils
Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies to identify pernicious anaemia
MRI of the spine showing high T2 signal in the dorsal columns (inverted V or dot sign)
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude copper deficiency mimicking the syndrome
Nerve conduction studies if a coexisting peripheral neuropathy is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive myelopathy causing gait failure or sphincter disturbance
Recent or repeated nitrous oxide use with acute neurological decline
Severe anaemia or pancytopenia requiring urgent evaluation
Coexisting cognitive decline suggesting advanced or long-standing deficiency
reference.prognosis: Recovery depends on how early replacement begins; symptoms present for less than a few months often improve substantially, whereas long-standing deficits may only stabilise, leaving residual sensory ataxia or spasticity.
pitfalls: Relying on a normal serum B12 and missing functional deficiency demonstrable by methylmalonic acid
Assuming anaemia must be present, thereby overlooking purely neurological presentations
Failing to ask about recreational or repeated medical nitrous oxide exposure
Overlooking copper deficiency, which produces an indistinguishable myelopathy
Attributing spastic-ataxic gait solely to spondylosis and delaying B12 assessment
management: Urgent vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin) replacement, initially by the parenteral route, started promptly to halt progression
Long-term maintenance cobalamin therapy, lifelong where the cause is pernicious anaemia or irreversible malabsorption
Identify and treat the underlying cause: pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, gastric surgery or dietary deficiency, with dietary advice or supplementation
Stop ongoing nitrous oxide exposure, which precipitates and worsens the disorder
Correct coexisting folate and iron deficiency, but replace B12 first to avoid precipitating neurological deterioration
Rehabilitation with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for residual sensory ataxia and spasticity, with falls prevention
Monitor the haematological and neurological response, escalating promptly since earlier treatment predicts better recovery
